name: dft_simd (vertical-SIMD FFTW codelets)
baseline: FFTW 3 (planner/execute API with its SSE/AVX codelets, single and 8-transform advanced interface)
workload: Forward real-to-complex DFT of 60 single-precision samples, 2**24 (16.8 million) waveforms, single core; the 2025 update adds a 1024-sample case with AVX2 and AVX512 codelets.
claimed_speedup: 2018 run: 8 transforms per call to the generated AVX 60-sample codelet took 379 ms, 'approximately five times faster than the fastest FFTW option' (FFTW 1912-1925 ms aligned, 3135 ms misaligned); fixed-stride version 207 ms. 2025 update (AMD EPYC 9474F, single core): 'In the 60-sample case the AVX2 codelet runs 10.8 times faster than using the FFW API'; 1024-sample AVX2 codelet 'about 1.6 times faster', AVX512 '2.3 times faster' (FFTW_Aligned_One 858 ms vs CODELET_AVX_FixedStride 79 ms for 60 samples, 12,136 ms vs 7,270 ms for 1024 AVX2, 24,657 ms vs 10,610 ms for 1024 AVX512; ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt sets -march=native, -O3 for Release and RelWithDebInfo, -std=c++11; README names Apple LLVM 9.0.0 (clang-900.0.39.2) on macOS High Sierra for the 2018 run; compiler for the 2025 EPYC run not stated.
hardware: 2018: MacBook Pro, Intel Core i5-5287U 2.90GHz (AVX2+FMA), FFTW from MacPorts; 2025: AMD EPYC 9474F, single core.
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in library: demonstration of adapting FFTW's genfft scalar codelets to SIMD vector types so that 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX512) independent transforms are processed per call ('vertical' SIMD). Only tiny fixed sizes (60 and 1024 real-to-complex single-precision); callers must batch and interleave data into vector lanes; x86 AVX2/AVX512 only (OpenCL variant is experimental); fixed-stride version trades runtime flexibility; codelets must be generated with FFTW's OCaml genfft, so code is GPL.
caveats: Very small repository by one author; FFTW version not stated (MacPorts in 2018, unspecified in 2025); EPYC compiler and flags for the 2025 numbers not stated; the headline 10.8x is the fixed-stride codelet against FFTW's aligned single-transform plan (derived: 858 ms / 79 ms), the plain AVX codelet is 5.8x on the same table; the 2018 FFTW run used SSE codelets rather than a full AVX plan; speedup applies to bulk small transforms, not to general FFT use.
found_via: Registry route (vcpkg, conan, PyPI, crates.io listings) produced no new claim-bearing C/C++ libraries; surfaced via WebFetch of GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/dft?l=c%2B%2B ('SIMD discrete Fourier transform tests and discussion')

name: FINUFFT (with cuFINUFFT)
baseline: NFFT3 (Chemnitz NUFFT library, built on FFTW); docs also name CMCL NUFFT
workload: 2D type-1 (adjoint) nonuniform FFT, the example from NFFT3's simple test migrated to FINUFFT, single thread, same output to all shown digits.
claimed_speedup: '2D type 1 (NFFT3) done in 0.589 s' versus '2D type 1 (FINUFFT) in 0.0787 s' with relative error 9.93e-14 versus 9.58e-14, 'plus a 7.5x speed-up. (Both use a single thread, tested on the same AMD 5700U laptop.)'. docs/related.rst: NFFT 'is significantly slower and/or more memory-intensive than FINUFFT' and CMCL NUFFT is 'Much (up to 50x even for one thread) slower than FINUFFT'.
stars_or_usage: 445 stars; PyPI packages finufft and cufinufft; Python/Julia/MATLAB/Fortran bindings
tradeoffs: Computes nonuniform FFTs (types 1-3, 1-3 dimensions) to a user-set tolerance, not a plain uniform FFT; uses FFTW or DUCC for the inner FFT (CMake builds); GPU library cuFINUFFT in the same repository; NFFT3 offers more transform kinds (inverse NUFFT, sphere, rotation group) that FINUFFT lacks.
caveats: Peer-review tier rests on the SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 41(5), C479-C504 (2019) paper cited in the README; the paper itself could not be opened (arXiv blocked here). The page figure is a single data point from a migration tutorial with no compiler or flags stated, NFFT3 version 3.5.4alpha. docs/related.rst says DUCC's NUFFT is faster than FINUFFT in some regimes. docs/performance.rst compares FINUFFT releases and FFT backends, not other libraries. Baseline is a NUFFT library, outside the listed FFTW/MKL/KissFFT incumbents.
found_via: PyPI listing: pypi.org/pypi/finufft/json and cufinufft (found by filtering the PyPI simple index for fft/nufft names); GitHub topic https://github.com/topics/nufft

name: TRON (TRajectory Optimized NUFFT)
baseline: gpuNUFFT (GPU NUFFT gridding library) and Fessler's Image Reconstruction Toolbox (IRT, MATLAB)
workload: Non-Cartesian MRI gridding and degridding for radial (linear and golden-angle) trajectories on an Nvidia GPU, the repository for the paper 'Trajectory Optimized Nufft: Faster Non-Cartesian MRI Reconstruction through Prior Knowledge and Parallel Architectures'.
claimed_speedup: 'TRON is 30x faster than gpuNUFFT (a fast GPU code) and 75x faster than the image reconstruction toolbox (IRT) of Fessler (a ubiquitous CPU-based Matlab code)'; also 'comprising 50% less code than the minimal subset of IRT tested'.
hardware: Nvidia CUDA GPU (model not stated on the page)
tradeoffs: Specialised to radial trajectories and CUDA (needs cuFFT, nvcc); gridding code only, not a general uniform FFT or arbitrary-trajectory NUFFT; reproducing the paper needs MATLAB, BART and gpuNUFFT.
caveats: Peer-review tier rests on the Magnetic Resonance in Medicine paper linked in the README (onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mrm.27497), which was not opened. GPU model, compiler and flags are not on the page, so not tier A. The speedups are for the gridding step against gpuNUFFT and IRT, not against FFTW/MKL/KissFFT, and the repository description ('radial Fast Fourier Transform') overstates it as an FFT. Latest commits (Jan 2026) only add zipped MATLAB files; the CUDA code dates from 2018-2021.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/fft?l=cuda (registry route gave no new claim-bearing libraries)

name: FFTW++ (implicit dealiased convolutions on FFTW3)
baseline: FFTW 3 with explicit zero-padded convolutions (and FFTW's MPI transpose for the distributed code)
workload: 2D and 3D dealiased (zero-padded) convolutions and FFTs built on FFTW3; implicit padding avoids transforming the padded zeros.
claimed_speedup: README: 'in 2D and 3D implicit zero-padding substantially reduces memory usage and computation time' (cites Bowman and Roberts, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 33:1 (2011); Roberts and Bowman, J. Comput. Phys. 356 (2018); Murasko and Bowman, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 46:3 (2024)). No numeric speedup appears on the page.
tradeoffs: Header library and MPI transposes on top of FFTW3 (so FFTW's GPL licence applies unless a commercial FFTW licence is used); the gain is specific to dealiased convolutions in 2D/3D, plain FFTs are plain FFTW calls; C, Fortran and Python wrappers for the convolution routines; mpi/fftw directory benchmarks the adaptive transpose against FFTW's MPI transpose.
caveats: No numbers on the repository page; the speedups are claimed in three peer-reviewed papers that could not be opened here (university PDFs and doi.org blocked), so the tier rests on the README's citations and a verifier should confirm the numbers. The baseline is explicit padding implemented by the same authors on top of FFTW, so this is an algorithmic win over a naive FFTW pipeline, not a faster FFT kernel. CPU, compiler and flags unknown.
found_via: vcpkg baseline.json then ports/fftwpp/vcpkg.json (description 'FFTW++ is a C++ header/MPI transpose for Version 3 of the highly optimized FFTW')

name: minfft
baseline: KissFFT (the README also plots PocketFFT and FFTW with SSE2 for reference)
workload: One-dimensional double-precision in-place forward complex DFT of power-of-two size N = 2^1 to 2^20, speed in Mflops (plot docs/speed.svg).
claimed_speedup: README: 'It achieves high performance by simple means' with speed plots against KissFFT and PocketFFT. Values digitised from the plot (derived from page data, approximate): minfft is above KissFFT at every size, roughly 1.4x to 4.8x and about 2x typical (about 8,400 vs 4,700 Mflops at N=2^8, 6,400 vs 3,700 at N=2^16, 1,700 vs 850 at N=2^20). minfft is faster than PocketFFT only up to about N=2^6 and slower than PocketFFT from 2^7 to 2^16; FFTW SSE2 is faster than minfft at every size.
tradeoffs: Power-of-two sizes only; double precision by default (MINFFT_SINGLE for float); scalar C99 code with split-radix kernels, no explicit SIMD; also provides real DFT and DCT/DST types 2-4, multi-dimensional transforms, a Fortran 2003 interface; very small (two source files).
caveats: First-party plot only; no CPU model, compiler or flags, and no benchmark program is documented in the README, so numbers are read off an SVG and approximate. It loses to FFTW (SSE2) at all sizes and to PocketFFT at mid sizes, so the real claim is 'small and faster than KissFFT'.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/cooley-tukey (registry route gave no new claim-bearing libraries)

name: cuSpFFT
baseline: cuFFT (dense 2D real-to-complex) and SpFFT (eth-cscs/SpFFT, CUDA backend)
workload: Single-precision 2D real-to-complex FFT of binary sparse matrices from SuiteSparse (benzene 8,219 x 8,219, density 0.36%), median of 10 runs after one warm-up, CUDA-event timing.
claimed_speedup: benzene: custom binary-sparse pipeline 14.65 ms vs dense cuFFT 23.64 ms ('1.61x faster, 10.7x less memory'); variant using cuFFT inside 9.60 ms ('2.46x faster, 10.4x less memory'); SpFFT about 32 ms ('0.74x speed'). pct20stif (52,329 x 52,329): dense cuFFT plan creation failed and SpFFT ran out of device memory, the sparse variants completed in 2,569 ms and 893 ms.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA Toolkit 12.5.82, CMake 3.20+, C++17, -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 24 GB (compute capability 8.9), driver 555.42.02, Linux x86_64; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Only for binary (all-ones) sparse 2D inputs in CSC form; Bluestein convolution at a smooth length; needs CUDA; the custom variant is less accurate than dense cuFFT (max_abs vs FFTW CPU reference 2.0e-01 vs 4.7e-02 on benzene).
caveats: Course project (CSC 766) with no licence file, so code must not be copied. The README itself reports losses: on sstmodel dense cuFFT is 0.85 ms vs 1.39 ms or 3.62 ms for the sparse variants, and on the power-of-2 delaunay_n14 matrix dense cuFFT takes 7.81 ms vs 68.56 ms and 304.76 ms. SpFFT figure is a single run. The baseline is a dense GPU FFT that the workload is deliberately unfavourable to; not a general FFT speedup.
found_via: GitHub topic pages https://github.com/topics/bluestein and https://github.com/topics/cufft (registry route gave no new claim-bearing libraries)

name: AOCL-FFTW (AMD-optimized FFTW)
baseline: FFTW 3.3.10 (upstream MIT/FFTW release it is derived from)
workload: General FFTs on AMD EPYC CPUs (Naples, Rome, Milan and later), including in-place MPI FFTs and large in-place transposes; no concrete workload given on the page.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the page. Qualitative claim in README_AMD.md: 'AOCL-FFTW achieves high performance as a result of its various optimizations involving improved SIMD Kernel functions, improved copy functions ..., improved 256-bit kernels selection by Planner and an optional in-place transpose for large problem sizes', a faster in-place MPI transpose, and a new fast planner mode that shortens planning time.
compiler_and_flags: configure --enable-sse2 --enable-avx --enable-avx2 --enable-avx512 --enable-mpi --enable-openmp --enable-shared --enable-amd-opt --enable-amd-mpifft --enable-dynamic-dispatcher (build recipe only, not a benchmark setup)
hardware: Targeted at AMD EPYC; no benchmark hardware stated
stars_or_usage: 64 stars; AMD's official FFT in AOCL, packaged downstream (for example an AUR fftw-amd package)
tradeoffs: Drop-in FFTW 3 API and feature set; GPL; optimised for AMD Zen with extra configure flags and a dynamic dispatcher for portable x86 builds; adds Top-N planner and AMD application optimisation layer.
caveats: Tier D: vendor claim with no numbers anywhere on the repository pages. AMD's own benchmark pages (amd.com, docs.amd.com) were blocked in this container, so no figures were seen. The page does not show a GitHub 'forked from' parent although the code is derived from FFTW 3.3.10, so is_fork_of is left null. Notable enough for the single allowed tier D entry.
found_via: WebSearch query 'AOCL-FFTW performance versus FFTW 3.3.10 AMD EPYC speedup benchmark'
